paras_en: The dollar rose on Thursday (the 1st), reaching a 17‑month high against the euro as a global bond sell‑off pushed U.S. and European government bond yields to fresh highs, while higher oil prices heightened market inflation concerns.
In the New York close, the dollar index (DXY), which tracks the greenback against six major currencies, rose 0.51% and at one point hit its highest level since April 2025.

As of the end of September, the dollar against a basket of currencies has risen for six consecutive quarters, marking the longest streak of gains since 2022. During 2022, U.S. rate hikes outpaced those of other countries.

The euro fell below $1.1215, its first dip below that level since May 2025. The dollar’s recent strength over the past months has been partly driven by a quarterly surge in U.S. Treasury yields—the largest since 1994.
The euro slipped 0.77% to $1.12433. In September the euro fell nearly 2.5%, the biggest monthly decline since July 2025.

NatWest Markets G10 FX strategy head Brian Daingerfield said, “Higher yields are the result of multiple factors, especially market worries about fiscal policy, including signs of weakness in the French bond market that could be spreading globally. In addition, markets remain concerned about rising energy prices and inflation.”

He added, “Markets expect central banks worldwide to keep tightening policy, including the Fed. In the past few days, after some personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data we released yesterday, that expectation eased a bit. Overall, however, the market broadly believes the Fed may still tighten further.”
U.S. 10‑year Treasury yields rose to their highest level since 2002 on the day, later easing 5.65 basis points to 5.237%.

The euro also fell against the yen and the Swiss franc, while it barely stayed positive against the pound. Concerns over France’s fiscal situation have spooked markets, sending French bond yields to a 14‑year high, and German benchmark bonds have also been sold off.
Klarity FX director Amo Sahota said, “For weeks the dollar has been consistently strong, and the market keeps coming up with new narratives that give the dollar further upside.”

“But I think the latest factor may be the most worrying—panic in European markets. French debt is simply too high, and the widening spread between France and Germany is unsettling everyone. The euro has therefore weakened sharply, and the decline is accelerating again.”

Wednesday’s data showed U.S. August inflation rose less than expected, and July’s figure was revised down, lowering market expectations for a Fed rate hike this month. However, euro‑area inflation surged, underscoring that rising energy prices continue to threaten the global economy.

Global bonds posted their biggest monthly drop in years in September, pushing yields higher. The drivers include deteriorating fiscal positions, an oversupply of sovereign debt, and warming inflation, among other factors.
The pound fell 0.49% to $1.32. It is down 2.1% in September but held steady against the euro. The euro‑pound rate is about 85.18 pence, the lowest since the end of June.
The yen weakened 0.41% to ¥158.07 per dollar.
The Australian dollar slipped to $0.69040, a three‑month low, after domestic inflation data came in below expectations.

paras_en: Today is the first trading day of the fourth quarter, showing a rally in both stocks and the exchange rate. The index closed at a historic high of 48,353.49 points. However, the New Taiwan dollar against the US dollar first depreciated then appreciated, slipping nearly 0.1 NT$ and breaking the 31.9 NT$ barrier, before ending at a modest 0.01 NT$ rise to 31.842 NT$ under a slight adjustment by the central bank, with total foreign‑exchange turnover in Taipei and Yuan‑Tai markets reaching US$2.558 billion.

The Taiwan stock market opened higher but volatile, briefly turning negative before foreign investors returned to net buying, expanding the rally. The weighted index finished up 413.36 points at 48,353.49, a new closing high, with foreign investors net buying NT$21.937 billion for the day. Large‑cap stocks such as TSMC and MediaTek rose across the board, and passive component and PCB groups became the market’s biggest money magnets.

The New Taiwan dollar opened at 31.87 NT$ per US$, peaked at 31.842 NT$, and fell to a low of 31.946 NT$. Foreign investors showed two‑way flows, while the central bank made a slight adjustment, narrowing the depreciation trend and closing at 31.842 NT$, a modest 0.01 NT$ increase.

Looking at major currencies against the US dollar, central‑bank data show the US Dollar Index up 0.45%, the Japanese yen down 0.95%, the Korean won down 0.75%, the Singapore dollar down 0.28%, and the New Taiwan dollar up 0.03%. The Chinese yuan was closed for the National Day holiday.

US inflation data showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rising 0.3% month‑over‑month, below the market expectation of 0.4%. According to CME’s FedWatch tool, traders now assign a 37% probability to a Fed rate hike in October, down from 70% a week earlier.
